nodes.title: Amazon S3: Key Ideas
nodes.content: S3 is AWS's object store — flat namespace of buckets containing objects, accessed via HTTP. It backs almost every AWS architecture: data lakes, static sites, backups, lambda triggers, CloudFront origins. The exam tests storage classes, encryption, access control, and event notifications.

flashcards.front: S3 storage classes — pick one for backups, one for hot data, one for archive.
flashcards.back: Hot: S3 Standard (high cost, instant access). Backups / infrequent: S3 Standard-IA (cheaper storage, retrieval fee). Archive: Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest storage, retrieval in hours). Lifecycle policies move objects between classes automatically based on age.

flashcards.front: S3 bucket policy vs IAM policy vs ACL — which to use?
flashcards.back: IAM policy: 'this user/role can read bucket X'. Bucket policy: 'these principals can access this bucket' — required for cross-account and public access. ACL (legacy): per-object permissions, mostly avoided today. Use bucket policies for most cross-account, IAM for in-account.

flashcards.front: How do you make an S3 website (static-site hosting)?
flashcards.back: Enable static-website hosting on the bucket, upload index.html, set a bucket policy allowing public-read on objects, point a CloudFront distribution at it for HTTPS + edge caching. Don't expose the bucket directly — CloudFront with an OAC (Origin Access Control) is the canonical pattern.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between server-side and client-side encryption?
flashcards.back: SSE: data encrypted by S3 after upload. Variants: SSE-S3 (AWS-managed key, easiest), SSE-KMS (your KMS key, audit trail), SSE-C (you supply the key on each request). Client-side: you encrypt before upload — S3 only sees ciphertext. Pick SSE-KMS for compliance, SSE-S3 for default-on.

questions.q: An application stores user-uploaded files in S3. Files are frequently accessed for the first 30 days, rarely accessed for the next 60 days, then never needed again. Which S3 lifecycle configuration minimizes storage cost?
choices: S3 Standard with no lifecycle policy, retaining objects for all 90+ days indefinitely
Store all objects in S3 Glacier Deep Archive from day 1 — including the first 30 days
Transition to S3 Standard-IA at day 30; expire at 90 days total
Apply S3 Intelligent-Tiering across all 90 days to auto-manage storage class
questions.explanation: S3 Standard-IA charges lower per-GB storage rates than Standard but adds a per-GB retrieval fee — an ideal trade-off once objects transition from frequent to infrequent access after day 30. Expiring objects at day 90 eliminates ongoing cost for data that will never be needed again. Keeping all 90+ days in S3 Standard pays the premium tier even after access frequency drops to near-zero. Glacier Deep Archive from day 1 imposes up to 12-hour retrieval delays during the first 30 days when files are frequently accessed — retrieval latency and fees during that window outweigh the storage savings. S3 Intelligent-Tiering adds a per-object monitoring fee that is wasted here because the access pattern is already known and a deterministic lifecycle transition is cheaper.

questions.q: A global software vendor needs to publish product documentation, images, and downloadable PDFs for a product launch microsite. The 3 GB file set is updated roughly once per month and must load quickly for visitors across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. The team has no dedicated server administrators and must minimize both cost and ongoing operational effort. Which architecture meets these requirements?
choices: Host the assets in S3 and distribute them through a CloudFront distribution with edge caching
Deploy file-serving EC2 instances in three regions behind Route 53 latency-based routing with Auto Scaling
Use Elastic Beanstalk to run a Node.js server that reads assets from an Amazon EFS volume
Place files in S3 and expose them through an Application Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing enabled
questions.explanation: S3 provides durable, serverless object storage with no servers to patch or scale, and CloudFront distributes content from hundreds of edge locations so visitors worldwide receive files from the nearest point of presence — achieving sub-100 ms load times with no compute to operate. Multi-region EC2 with latency-based DNS achieves geographic proximity but requires capacity planning, OS patching, Auto Scaling configuration, and 24/7 operations in each region — directly violating the 'no dedicated administrators' constraint. Elastic Beanstalk running a Node.js server in front of EFS introduces a single-region compute tier and per-server filesystem latency, neither of which gives global users edge proximity. An Application Load Balancer cannot use S3 as a native origin, performs no edge caching, and would still require backend compute to serve the files.

questions.q: A company runs a compliance archival system where regulatory documents are uploaded once and retrieved at most once per year for audits. The compliance team's primary constraint is storage cost, not retrieval speed. Which S3 storage class is most appropriate?
choices: S3 Standard-IA — millisecond reads, $0.0125/GB-month plus retrieval fee
S3 One Zone-IA — single AZ, lower redundancy, millisecond access
S3 Glacier Deep Archive — 12-hour retrieval, $0.00099/GB-month
S3 Standard — multi-AZ, immediate access, $0.023/GB-month
questions.explanation: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost S3 storage class at roughly $0.00099 per GB-month, designed for data accessed at most once or twice per year with retrieval time up to 12 hours. For annual compliance audits where retrieval latency is irrelevant, this is the cost-optimal choice. S3 Standard costs roughly 23× more per GB and provides immediate retrieval that the workload does not need. Standard-IA still costs more per GB than Glacier and charges a per-retrieval fee that hurts when auditors pull large object sets at once. One Zone-IA is cheaper than Standard-IA but still far more expensive than Deep Archive and sacrifices multi-AZ durability without offering archival-tier pricing.

questions.q: A media sharing platform lets users upload large video files from a browser. Currently all uploads pass through the application server tier before being written to S3, creating bandwidth bottlenecks and high EC2 costs during peak hours. The security team requires that upload credentials expire no more than 15 minutes after issuance. Which solution removes the application server from the upload data path while meeting the security requirement?
choices: Deploy AWS Transfer Family with SFTP fronting the application fleet to handle every browser upload at scale
Route every upload through API Gateway as a binary passthrough that the application server still proxies internally
Open the S3 bucket for public PUT access and rely on a static 15-minute token shared with the browser
Have the application server return a 15-minute presigned S3 PUT URL so the browser uploads directly
questions.explanation: A presigned PUT URL embeds the uploader's identity and expiry into a signed request URL. The application server generates the URL without ever touching file bytes, hands it to the browser, and the browser PUTs the file straight to S3 — eliminating the EC2 bandwidth bottleneck. Setting the URL TTL to 15 minutes satisfies the credential-lifetime requirement. AWS Transfer Family fronting the existing fleet still terminates uploads on the same EC2 instances, so the bottleneck remains. API Gateway as a binary passthrough imposes a 10 MB request-body cap and re-introduces a server hop for every byte. Public PUT access on the bucket violates least privilege and lets any URL holder overwrite arbitrary objects.

questions.q: A healthcare startup stores de-identified patient records in S3. A new compliance framework requires (1) a verifiable log of every encryption key use, and (2) the ability to immediately revoke read access to all stored records during a security incident. The startup uses AWS KMS for key management. Which S3 server-side encryption configuration satisfies both requirements?
choices: SSE-S3 using the Amazon-managed S3 key (no KMS dependency)
SSE-KMS with the aws/s3 AWS-managed KMS key for the account
SSE-KMS with a dedicated company-owned KMS key and key policy
Client-side encryption using a key fetched from AWS Secrets Manager
questions.explanation: SSE-KMS with a customer-owned KMS key records every GenerateDataKey and Decrypt call in CloudTrail, providing the verifiable key-usage log required by the compliance framework. Disabling the company-owned key immediately prevents all future decrypts of every object encrypted with it, satisfying the instant-revoke requirement. SSE-S3 uses an Amazon-managed key with no per-call CloudTrail visibility and no customer-controlled lifecycle, so neither requirement is met. The aws/s3 AWS-managed KMS key logs KMS events but is owned by AWS — the company cannot disable it, so instant revocation of all read access is impossible. Client-side encryption with a Secrets Manager key shifts encryption out of S3 entirely and doesn't generate the same S3-side audit trail; revoking access also requires rotating the secret in every client process.

questions.q: A financial services company stores sensitive compliance reports in an S3 bucket that is accessed from multiple AWS accounts within the same AWS Organization. After an internal audit, the security team needs a control that prevents any principal outside the organization from accessing the bucket — even if an IAM policy in a member account is later misconfigured. Which S3 feature most directly satisfies this requirement?
choices: S3 Object Ownership set to Bucket Owner Enforced mode with no resource policy change
S3 Block Public Access policy enabled at the AWS Organization's management account
S3 bucket policy with the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key
IAM permission boundary policy applied to every user across the AWS Organization
questions.explanation: A bucket policy that uses the aws:PrincipalOrgID global condition key restricts access so that only principals belonging to the specified AWS Organization can make requests, acting as an organization-wide perimeter regardless of individual IAM grants in member accounts. S3 Object Ownership in Bucket Owner Enforced mode disables ACLs and consolidates ownership but does not, by itself, prevent out-of-organization principals from accessing the bucket. IAM permission boundaries constrain what a single IAM entity can do but cannot enforce cross-account access restrictions for every account in an organization. S3 Block Public Access prevents anonymous (unauthenticated) access but does not block authenticated requests from principals outside the organization.

nodes.title: Identity and access management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IAM is the layer that decides who can do what. It's almost always the first thing to misconfigure and the most common security failure mode. Every cloud uses the same primitives — identities, policies, roles — under slightly different names.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
flashcards.back: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are — password, MFA, certificate. Authorization (AuthZ) decides what you're allowed to do once authenticated — policies, roles, ACLs. AuthN happens first; AuthZ is checked on every request.

flashcards.front: What is a role (vs a user)?
flashcards.back: A user is a long-lived identity tied to a person. A role is a short-lived, assumable identity — services or users 'become' the role to get temporary credentials. Roles let you grant access without sharing long-term keys. Always prefer roles.

Identity-based policies attach to a user / role and say what THEY can do. Resource-based policies attach to a thing (S3 bucket, KMS key, SQS queue) and say who can access IT. Cross-account access usually needs both: target's resource policy says 'allow this account', source identity policy says 'allow this action on that resource'.

Instead of creating cloud users for every employee, federate from your corporate identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace). Users sign in once with their work account; the IdP issues a SAML / OIDC token; the cloud trades it for temporary credentials. One source of truth, instant deprovisioning.

questions.q: A DevOps engineer discovers that an EC2 web application is calling S3 using access keys stored in a plaintext configuration file on the instance. The security team requires these long-lived credentials to be removed immediately while preserving S3 read access. What should the solutions architect recommend?
choices: Create a dedicated IAM user, deploy its credentials to the instance via environment variables
Store the credentials as SecureString parameters in SSM and pull them on each instance boot
Rotate the access keys and redeploy the instance image with updated credential values
Attach an IAM role to the instance and remove all hard-coded access keys
questions.explanation: Attaching an IAM role to an EC2 instance causes the instance metadata service (IMDS) to vend temporary, automatically-rotated credentials — no static keys exist on the instance to be stolen or leaked, and the application calls S3 using the same SDK with no code change. Creating a dedicated IAM user and shipping its access keys via environment variables simply moves the same long-lived secret to a different filesystem location; the credential is still static and leakable. SSM SecureString parameters are KMS-encrypted at rest, but the long-lived IAM-user key inside the parameter is still a static credential that must be rotated manually. Rotating and redeploying the keys reduces the exposure window but does not eliminate the fundamental static-credential risk the security team flagged.

questions.q: A company's security policy requires that IAM users cannot perform any AWS API action in the current session unless they authenticated with their MFA device — not just their password — during that session. An IAM user who logs in with only username and password must be blocked from all API calls. Which control enforces this at the API request level?
choices: CloudTrail alarm firing on API calls made without MFA token
IAM Deny statement on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent = false
AWS Config managed rule checking MFA activation per user
IAM password policy set to require MFA device registration
questions.explanation: An IAM policy with `Effect: Deny, Action: *` and condition `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent: false` blocks all API calls in sessions where MFA was not used, regardless of what other policies allow. The user can authenticate but cannot take any action until they use their MFA device — enforcement happens at the API request level, not just at sign-in. A CloudTrail alarm is a detective control: it fires after the call has succeeded, not before, so it cannot block API actions. An AWS Config rule reports whether each user has an MFA device enabled but does not gate per-request access. An IAM password policy can require MFA device registration during account setup but does not enforce per-request MFA at the API level after login.

questions.q: A fintech company's SOC 2 audit requires that third-party auditors, who operate their own separate AWS account, have read-only access to specific S3 buckets for a two-week review window. The security team's constraints are: no long-lived credentials may be created, and no bucket endpoint may be exposed to the public internet. What should they configure?
choices: Create an IAM user per auditor and email the access keys to each
Create a cross-account IAM role and share its ARN with the auditors
Share presigned S3 URLs (2-week expiry) directly with each auditor
Create a new AWS account for auditors and assign root-level S3 access
questions.explanation: A cross-account IAM role with an S3 read-only policy and a trust policy scoped to the auditor's AWS account lets the auditors call sts:AssumeRole to obtain short-lived temporary credentials — no long-lived keys are created or shared. Deleting the role at the end of the review instantly revokes all access. Creating an IAM user per auditor and emailing access keys produces long-lived credentials that may be forwarded or cached, violating the no-permanent-credentials requirement. Creating a new AWS account just for auditors with root-level S3 access grants far more privilege than required and creates a long-lived shared account. Presigned URLs are publicly accessible HTTPS endpoints — anyone who holds the URL can fetch the object — and cannot be scoped to a specific external AWS account, failing both security constraints.

questions.q: A web application runs on an EC2 instance with an instance profile granting s3:* on all resources and ec2:* on all resources. A security review shows the application only ever performs object retrieval from a single S3 bucket named 'prod-assets'. The team wants to reduce the blast radius if the instance is compromised. Which IAM change should a solutions architect implement?
choices: Add an explicit Deny on s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject for prod-assets and remove ec2:* assets to limit scope
Remove ec2:* entirely and replace s3:* with s3:GetObject scoped to the 'prod-assets' bucket ARN
Attach a permissions boundary that limits the instance to S3 read-only on any bucket
Enable IAM Access Analyzer and archive bucket findings for the instance profile
questions.explanation: Least privilege requires granting only the exact permissions actually needed. Removing ec2:* entirely (the application makes no EC2 API calls) and replacing s3:* with s3:GetObject on the specific bucket ARN directly eliminates the excess permissions and shrinks the blast radius if the instance is compromised. Adding Deny statements for selected S3 writes is weaker — the broad s3:* Allow remains, so any new S3 API added by AWS in the future is automatically granted until someone updates the policy. A permissions boundary constrains the ceiling of what the role could be granted, but does not remove the existing broad Allow inside the role's policy. IAM Access Analyzer flags overly permissive findings but does not modify the underlying policy.

correct.useCase: Durable block-level volumes attached to a single EC2 instance — like a virtual hard disk you can snapshot.

distractors.useCase: Object storage for static website assets and backups.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: An online gaming platform stores a real-time leaderboard mapping player IDs to scores and ranks. During peak tournament events, the service handles 600,000 read operations per minute and every lookup is by a single player ID — no aggregations or joins are required. Response latency must stay under 5 milliseconds as player count is expected to triple over the next year. Which AWS database service is the best fit?
choices: Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity mode
Amazon Aurora MySQL with a Multi-AZ standby and provisioned IOPS
Amazon Redshift with result-set caching enabled for repeated queries
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached used as the authoritative data store
questions.explanation: DynamoDB is purpose-built for high-throughput, low-latency key lookups at any scale — on-demand capacity automatically adjusts to handle unpredictable peak volumes without manual provisioning, and single-digit millisecond performance is maintained regardless of table size. Aurora MySQL is a relational engine optimized for transactional queries with joins; matching DynamoDB's sub-5ms key-lookup latency at 600k requests/minute requires significant tuning overhead and dedicated read replicas, making it a poor fit for this simple, high-volume access pattern. Redshift is an OLAP data warehouse designed for analytical scans across large datasets, not single-key point lookups at low latency. ElastiCache for Memcached is an in-memory cache without durability — data is lost on node restart or eviction, making it unsuitable as the authoritative store for a leaderboard that must persist through failures.

questions.q: A financial reporting service writes an account balance to DynamoDB and immediately performs a read to return the updated value to the client. Testers consistently observe stale values — the read returns the pre-update balance. The development team wants to fix this in code without changing the table design or data model. What change should they make?
choices: Set ConsistentRead=true on every GetItem and Query call against the table
Switch table reads to a Global Secondary Index scoped to the account partition
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table for cached reads
Replace GetItem with a Query that uses a FilterExpression on the balance attribute of the same table
questions.explanation: Setting ConsistentRead=true forces DynamoDB to read from the partition's leader node and return data that reflects all writes acknowledged before the read, eliminating the stale-read window that exists under eventually consistent (default) mode. Switching reads to a Global Secondary Index makes the situation worse — GSIs do not support strongly consistent reads at all, regardless of the ConsistentRead flag. DAX caches reads in memory and would also worsen the problem; it would serve the cached pre-update value until its TTL expires rather than the freshly written value. Replacing GetItem with a Query that uses a FilterExpression still reads the base table with the same default consistency, so stale results remain possible.

questions.q: A fintech company stores payment transactions in DynamoDB. For regulatory compliance, every item modification must be captured in an immutable audit log showing both the old and new attribute values. The solution must not require changes to the existing application, which writes directly to DynamoDB. Which approach creates a complete item-level change history?
choices: DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery with hourly snapshot comparisons
DynamoDB Streams consumed by Lambda, writing events to S3
DynamoDB on-demand backup job triggered by an EventBridge rule
DynamoDB Global Tables replicating to an audit-only AWS region
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Streams records every INSERT, MODIFY, and REMOVE event at the item level, including both the old and new attribute images, with no changes needed in the writing application. A Lambda function triggered by the stream writes each event record to S3 (with a Glacier or Object Lock layer for immutability), creating a per-modification audit trail. Point-in-Time Recovery lets you restore the entire table to a past moment but does not expose a log of individual change events. Global Tables replicate data across regions for active-active access without tracking what changed. On-demand backups capture full table snapshots rather than per-modification records, so the team would have to diff entire tables to reconstruct change history.

questions.q: A security audit finds that a Lambda function processing payment records connects to an RDS PostgreSQL database using the publicly accessible endpoint. The security team requires the database to be unreachable from the internet while Lambda retains the ability to execute queries. What configuration achieves this?
choices: Remove RDS public access and restrict connections via a security policy scoped to Lambda's execution role
Create a VPC peering connection and a security group that routes Lambda traffic into the private RDS subnet
Deploy Lambda inside the VPC and configure the RDS security group to allow access from the Lambda security group
Keep RDS publicly accessible, harden the network security group, and rotate credentials hourly via Secrets Manager
questions.explanation: Configuring Lambda with VPC settings creates an ENI in the specified subnets, allowing Lambda to reach RDS over private IP addresses — no public endpoint required. Disabling RDS public accessibility ensures no internet-originating connection can reach the database. Removing public access and relying on an execution-role 'security policy' does not work because RDS network access is governed by VPC security groups, not by IAM roles attached to the caller. VPC peering connects two VPCs at the network layer but cannot bridge a public-only Lambda to a private subnet — Lambda must still have an ENI in a routable VPC to use private addressing. Keeping RDS publicly accessible with a hardened security group and hourly credential rotation still leaves a reachable internet endpoint, violating the explicit requirement.

questions.q: An image-processing service is triggered by S3 uploads and runs on AWS Lambda. High-resolution RAW camera files have started arriving that require 22 minutes of CPU-intensive processing — seven minutes beyond Lambda's hard 15-minute execution limit. The team wants to keep a serverless approach. What is the BEST architectural fix?
choices: Replace the Lambda function with an ECS Fargate task that runs the same image to bypass the timeout
Move the workload to an EC2 Auto Scaling Group with a queue-driven job pattern for long-running jobs
Increase Lambda memory to 10,240 MB and rely on the proportional vCPU bump to finish under 15 minutes
Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate Lambda invocations that each process a chunk of the image
questions.explanation: Step Functions splits a long job into stages that each fit inside Lambda's 15-minute ceiling, while the state machine handles sequencing, retries, and intermediate state — preserving the serverless model and getting around the hard timeout. ECS Fargate would also clear the timeout, but it abandons the serverless approach the team wants to keep (tasks, networking, and scaling rules now have to be managed). An EC2 Auto Scaling Group is an even larger step away from serverless and requires AMI / OS lifecycle ownership. Maxing Lambda memory to 10,240 MB speeds CPU-bound work but cannot extend the 15-minute execution ceiling, so a 22-minute job still fails.

questions.q: A team's serverless checkout API runs on API Gateway backed by Lambda. During a flash sale, multiple functions in the same AWS account exhaust the shared regional concurrency pool, leaving the checkout function throttled while lower-priority background functions remain active. The team wants to guarantee the checkout function always has a minimum concurrency allocation that other functions in the account cannot claim. Which Lambda feature addresses this?
choices: Reserved concurrency set on the checkout Lambda function
Provisioned concurrency for the checkout Lambda function
AWS Lambda Power Tuning to reduce per-invocation duration
API Gateway usage plan throttling per customer API key
questions.explanation: Reserved concurrency carves out a dedicated slice of the account-level concurrency pool exclusively for the specified function. Other functions cannot consume that reserved portion, ensuring the checkout function is never starved by lower-priority workloads competing for the shared pool. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes execution environments to eliminate cold starts but does not prevent other functions from consuming the unreserved portion of the account-wide limit, so checkout can still be throttled at peak. Lambda Power Tuning helps right-size memory for per-invocation cost/latency but does not guarantee minimum concurrent capacity. API Gateway usage plans throttle individual external API keys but have no effect on how Lambda allocates its internal concurrency pool across functions.

questions.q: A financial application processes wire transfer instructions from an SQS queue using a Lambda function. After a code deployment, certain message formats cause the Lambda function to throw an unhandled exception. These messages are returned to the queue, immediately retried, and continue failing — consuming Lambda invocations while delaying valid messages. What should the solutions architect implement?
choices: Configure a Dead Letter Queue with maxReceiveCount=3 and a CloudWatch alarm on DLQ depth
Switch the source queue to FIFO so wire transfers are processed in strict order with the same retry policy
Increase the visibility timeout to 5 minutes so Lambda has more time to process each message
Extend the message retention period to 14 days so failing messages are not deleted automatically
questions.explanation: A Dead Letter Queue receives messages that exceed maxReceiveCount processing attempts, permanently removing them from the main queue so they stop consuming Lambda invocations and blocking healthy traffic. A CloudWatch alarm on DLQ depth alerts the team when failures accumulate, enabling rapid root-cause investigation. Switching to a FIFO source preserves message order but does nothing to stop a poison-pill message from cycling endlessly — strict ordering actually makes the problem worse, because a single failing message halts every later message in the same MessageGroupId. Increasing the visibility timeout just delays each retry; the bad message still cycles back once the timeout expires. Extending retention to 14 days lengthens the failure window rather than terminating it.

questions.q: A company's analytics portal lets users request custom PDF reports that take 8–12 minutes to generate. The architecture must return an immediate acknowledgment to the browser, continue generating the report in the background, and notify the user via SNS when the report is ready. API Gateway has a hard 29-second integration timeout. Which pattern meets all three requirements?
choices: HTTP long-poll connection held open until report finishes; user sees a spinner the whole time
Async SQS queue with worker plus an SNS completion topic that emails the user
Extend API Gateway integration timeout past 29 s; user request blocks until report is done
Browser polls a Lambda status endpoint every 10 s and shows status to the user
questions.explanation: An SQS-backed async pattern decouples the browser request from the long-running job: the frontend enqueues the request and immediately receives a job ID, a background worker processes the PDF, and SNS sends a notification when the report is ready. API Gateway's 29-second integration timeout makes a long-poll connection impossible — the proxy will close the connection long before the 8–12 minute job finishes. The integration timeout cannot be raised past 29 s, so 'extending' it is not actually a configuration option. Polling every 10 seconds works for status but wastes compute on the user's device and still requires a separate completion notification mechanism — it doesn't satisfy the immediate-acknowledgment + push-notify pattern as cleanly.

finalBoss.title: Final Exam: AWS Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03)
